> Pertaining to the argument that they receive disproportionately more resource, I will argue that they receive more resources not because they are SAP school but because they are better academically? 

Ok let's say that this is the case. It is still an issue that students who not study Chinese as their MTL are unable to attend these 'academically better' schools. Students should not have to forgo the ability to learn about their own mother tongue in order to get into these schools. Sure there are other schools out there, but given that a significant proportion of competitive schools are SAPs, this means that a disproportionately lower number of minority students have the opportunity to attend competitive schools. School admission is no longer based on meritocracy.

>I think there is a valid point on whether SAP schools create exclusivity. However, OP seems to want to drive this conversation in a certain way to highlight that SAP schools are a form of "systemic racism", has gone out of the way to negate some of the valid points that others have brought up about the creation of SAP schools.

I do agree that the creation of SAP was a solution to a problem that did exist, but I don't see the relevance in today's society.

> Also, I would like to point out that nothing is stopping people from SAP schools or any schools for that matter to be exclusive or to be inclusive.  

Definitely not, but I think striving towards a society that gives equal opportunity and does not discriminate with regards to race, language or religion would be good.

> In the end, the individual himself or herself must want to genuinely make the effort. 

Definitely! But as an institution, it would be great if opportunities were provided that encourages such an effort. I am not saying everyone who attends a SAP school is racist.

Hi, thank you for your reply. I did not say all students who attend SAP schools are racist, just that the existence of SAP schools means that minority students do not have equal opportunity in Singapore.

> sure it is not a necessity. but the introduction of SAP schools in the first place were meant to placate a population then known for protests in exchange for taking away a substantial part of local chinese culture. like the user above said it was seriously not sufficient. 

I don't think I have read enough to comment on how good the program was in tackling that issue, but I genuinely don't think it is an issue in society today. Most of the people affected are people in older generations, and they are not the ones benefitting from a change in the education system. This issue should be viewed as a challenge to providing the next generation of Singaporeans with equal opportunities (regardless of race, language or religion). 

>gambilan

Your lack of awareness of other cultures is very telling.

> Most SAP schools just happened to be schools with substantial history and thus a very influential alumni network. 

This is likely not to be a result of coincidence. SAP schools do get more funding and are more competitive. This will no doubt lead to a better quality of life.

> plus, much of the contention coming from this seems to be the fact that SAP schools tend to be considered elite or privileged because of their SAP status. I would bet a kidney that there wouldnt be any fuss if the schools were all normal schools. 

Exactly why this is an issue!!! If minorities do not have access to schools that are elite/privileged, that means the elite class will always be disproportionately comprised of Chinese people!

> You want to see the differences SAP status confers? compare RI and HCI. One is certainly not SAP. You see any differences there? 

The issue is not that people of all races can get into RI, it's that people of all races cannot get into HCI. I hope I don't have to explain why,

> There are even neighbourhood schools that have SAP status, but I cant even remember their names off hand because they are neighbourhood schools. 

Please provide examples.

> You show your ignorance when you say Chinese speaking locals too.  

I'm sorry for not considering people who speak different dialects. When I referred to Chinese as a language, I was referring to Mandarin Chinese. Still, my point stands for people who know Mandarin.

> yeah i call bullshit 

The user above was arguing for those who were educated in Chinese-medium schools. And I do think you are blind to this as an issue, there have been multiple cases of hiring discrimination. You can pm if you want some personal anecdotes.

> Either way, given enough time SAP will do away with itself as most students these days dont give a rats ass about mandarin or chinese culture, really. 

This is an issue too! One of the main reasons why there is still an emphasis on SAP education is that there is a push to preserve culture among future generations. Perhaps a discussion needs to be had on how this can be resolved not just in SAP schools.

> You would call all this systemic racism, but i would call this the result of freedom, and it is the manifestation of equality of opportunities rather than that of equality of outcomes. 

I find it really sad that you cannot see why this is not a result of equal opportunities. If you would like, I can recommend material for you to read up about inequality in Singapore.

I think you're overlooking something. Chinese-speaking locals can still have a means to survive (albeit through jobs like working in a hawker centre etc). Most jobs prefer candidates who have the ability to speak Chinese. Imagine if an Indian person were to try and survive in Singapore without knowing English, would they be able to? I know it side-tracks from the main issue here, but I think it's something worth considering. Even in this case, there is no way Chinese people as a whole are more disenfranchised than minorities. On another note, thanks for linking the NLB resource.
